knowledgeAnswers.rationale: Proceeding on a client's word, or testing by scratching, breaks the identification rule. Stopping, recording the basis and referring is the required outcome when the material cannot be identified.
Terrazzo aggregate may contain crystalline silica, so terrazzo is treated as silica-containing until its composition is known. It is not automatically natural stone or engineered stone.
Product labels, installer documents and written confirmation from the responsible person are acceptable bases. Scratching, grinding and cutting create silica dust and change the surface.
Identification must be confirmed and recorded before surface assessment. Client confidence and a technician's impression do not meet the rule.
Appearance cues only tell the technician when to stop and check. A documented basis is needed to identify the material.

practicalCriteria: Identifies the material from documents and non-destructive observation only
Records the identification basis and photographs the surface, labels and marks
Stops and escalates when the material cannot be identified
Refuses any scratch, grind or cut test on the surface
passRule: Knowledge checks: 4 of 5 correct (80%). Practical sign-off is separate and is not granted by the knowledge check: an assessor must observe every critical practical criterion and record it.
evidenceRequired: Dated photographs of the surface, labels and marks
Identification record with basis and decision
stopWorkCriteria: Material that cannot be identified, or possibly engineered stone
Any scratch, grind or cut used to identify the surface
Pressure to proceed without a documented basis
